attributionNote.claim: AI shows up as a reason because companies say so when they announce cuts. Challenger records the reason the company gives; it does not check it.
attributionNote.counter: Some analysts read part of these cuts as restructuring for other reasons. Harvard Business School researchers, interviewed for an article republished by HBS Working Knowledge, argue that AI has not yet caused widespread layoffs because most firms are still slow to put it to work. A separate Harvard Business Review analysis, based on a survey of 1,006 executives, argues that companies are cutting jobs for what they expect AI to do, not for what it has shown it can do. Challenger itself said Amazon's 16,000 January cuts appeared to be due more to over-hiring and removing management layers than to the new technology.

sources.name: Sy Boles, "AI Hasn't Spurred Widespread Layoffs Yet. Why Not?", Harvard Business School Working Knowledge (first published in the Harvard Gazette), 20 October 2026
Thomas H. Davenport and Laks Srinivasan, "Companies Are Laying Off Workers Because of AI's Potential—Not Its Performance", Harvard Business Review, 29 January 2026
Challenger, Gray & Christmas — Job Cut Report, January 2026

trend.text: Two things are true at once. All announced job cuts are down on 2025: 573,195 through September against 946,426 a year earlier (down 15% if government cuts are left out). Cuts that companies attribute to AI are up: 120,136 through September, more than twice the 54,836 for all of 2025.

layoffs.scopeNote: These two trackers measure different things. Challenger's US tech-sector count (165,925, January to September 2026) and Layoffs.fyi's global tech count use different scopes and methods, so their numbers are not comparable with each other.
